questions.stem: A student wants the ratio of phenotypes among offspring. Where does it come from?

options.explanation: Sizes are irrelevant; the grid is the source.
The ratio falls out of the cell counts.

questions.stem: Why write the parental genotypes first?

options.text: The square splits whatever alleles the parents actually carry, so an error there ruins every cell
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The reason is genetic, not cosmetic.
Parental genotypes are fixed.

options.text: Because the grid ignores the parents
options.explanation: The grid is built entirely from them.

questions.stem: List the steps for building a Punnett square.
questions.modelAnswer: Write the parental genotypes, split their alleles around the grid edges, fill the four inner cells, and read the offspring combinations.

questions.stem: State what a Punnett square shows.
questions.modelAnswer: It shows the possible allele combinations the offspring could receive, from which ratios and probabilities follow.

questions.stem: Explain why the square predicts probabilities rather than guarantees.
questions.modelAnswer: Each fertilisation is random, so the grid gives the chance of each outcome per pregnancy, not a promise about any particular child.

questions.stem: A breeder crosses two rabbits both known to be heterozygous for a single coat-colour gene. Describe how you would lay out the diagram before any mating happens.
questions.modelAnswer: Write both parental genotypes as heterozygous pairs, split the alleles around the grid edges, fill the four inner cells with the offspring combinations, and count the resulting ratio.

questions.stem: Show the F1 result of crossing tt with TT in words.
questions.modelAnswer: Every offspring receives T from one parent and t from the other, so all F1 plants are the tall heterozygotes Tt.

questions.stem: State which allele is dominant in pea height.
questions.modelAnswer: The tall allele T is dominant over the recessive short allele t.

questions.stem: Explain why no short plants appear in the F1 generation.
questions.modelAnswer: Every F1 plant inherits the dominant T from the tall parent, so the recessive t cannot express itself in any of them.

questions.stem: A farmer buys seed from a pure-breeding short strain and a pure-breeding tall strain. Predict the appearance of the entire first crop grown from crossing them.
questions.modelAnswer: Every first-generation plant receives one tall and one short allele, so the whole crop grows tall with no short plants appearing.

questions.stem: Derive the 3:1 ratio from the Tt by Tt grid.
questions.modelAnswer: The grid gives one TT, two Tt and one tt, and since Tt plants are tall, three cells are tall to every one short cell.

questions.stem: State the probability of a short offspring from Tt crossed with tt.
questions.modelAnswer: The probability is one half, or 50 percent.

questions.stem: Explain why the recessive characteristic resurfaces in the F2 after hiding in the F1.
questions.modelAnswer: The F1 plants each carry a hidden t allele, so when two of them breed, some offspring receive t from both parents and express the recessive short form.

questions.stem: A grower crosses an unknown tall plant with a short plant and gets half tall, half short offspring. What does the outcome reveal about the unknown parent, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The unknown tall parent must be heterozygous, because a homozygous tall parent could only have produced all tall offspring against the short partner.

questions.stem: Convert the 3:1 phenotypic ratio into percentages.
questions.modelAnswer: Three tall cells out of four give 75 percent tall, and the single short cell gives 25 percent short.

questions.stem: State the genotype ratio hidden behind the 3:1 phenotype ratio.
questions.modelAnswer: It is one TT to two Tt to one tt.

questions.stem: Explain why predictions from a Punnett square improve decisions in breeding programmes.
questions.modelAnswer: The grid quantifies the chance of each phenotype before any cross is performed, so breeders can pick parental genotypes that maximise the trait they want.

questions.stem: Two heterozygous pea plants are crossed and the grower plants exactly one seed. State the probability that this single plant is short.
questions.modelAnswer: The probability is 25 percent, the one short cell out of the four, independent of what any sibling would have shown.
